A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EHR-D3PM study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–C are readable, allowing relocated material and revised experimental coverage to be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments on MIMIC-III, D1 and D2, including fidelity, downstream prediction, membership inference and guided data augmentation results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds TabDDPM/TabSyn comparisons and attribute-inference measurements.

M1.justification: The multinomial diffusion process, Linformer-based denoiser, training objective and KL-regularized latent Langevin guidance are retained. Equation (4) uses compressed notation, while the architecture diagram and accompanying implementation description remain equivalent. Testing additional medical-code types does not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: D2 expands from 993 ICD features in v1 to 2,683 features comprising 993 ICD, 690 CPT and 1,000 GEN codes in v2 (Section 5.1, Appendix A.1 and D2 figures). This substantially broadens the clinical information represented in generation experiments, although the patient cohorts and six disease-prediction targets remain the same.

E2.justification: v2 adds TabDDPM to fidelity, utility and privacy comparisons, and TabSyn to MIMIC/D1 distribution comparisons. TabDDPM is sometimes printed as TabPPDM in utility tables. MIMIC/D1 plots replace the two GAN comparators with these diffusion models; D2 plots replace Med-WGAN with TabDDPM. Both GAN methods remain in numerical tables.

E3.justification: New protocols include attribute inference with 256 exposed attributes and weighted F1 scoring, plus TabSyn tests using the first 100 versus 200/full dimensions. Appendix A.3 specifies 500 diffusion steps and five denoising layers for the added baselines. Existing classification and augmentation protocols are retained. MCAD was already evaluated in v1 Table 11.

E4.justification: v2 adds attribute-inference attack analysis and a qualitative dimensionality-sensitivity finding: TabSyn works on 100 features but deteriorates at 200/full dimensions. The latter is not accompanied by a detailed numerical sensitivity sweep. Existing rare-code analyses and guided-versus-unconditional augmentation comparisons remain.

E5.justification: v2 Table 4 adds uncertainty terms to disease prevalences previously reported as point estimates in v1 Table 3. Their estimation procedure is unspecified. The classification protocol remains 50 bootstraps using 80% of test data. Fidelity and MIR intervals already existed in v1 appendices; reorganized fidelity tables lose their explicit 95% interval labeling.

E6.justification: Substantial new entries cover TabDDPM, TabSyn and attribute inference; v2 Table 3 reports EHR-D3PM AIR values of 0.020, 0.068 and 0.078 on MIMIC, D1 and D2. D2 plots report results under expanded code coverage, preventing direct same-setting comparisons. Most inherited table means remain, while some CMD uncertainty values change, including D1 EHR-D3PM from 0.028 to 0.026.

T1.justification: The ELBO, diffusion distributions, conditional factorization, latent-space guidance reasoning and Appendix C derivation are retained. Equation edits concern notation and typesetting. No substantive mathematical assumptions, proofs, propositions or derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract extends the privacy claim from reduced membership vulnerability to reduced attribute and membership vulnerability. The central contributions—discrete EHR diffusion, training-free conditional guidance, rare-condition generation and downstream augmentation—retain their previous meaning.

C2.justification: New limitations explicitly identify absent longitudinal modeling and untested advanced privacy attacks. Section 5.4 replaces v1's claim of lower MIR across all datasets with relatively low risks and explains that low attack scores can reflect failure to learn the data distribution. v2 also suggests sparsity as a cause of TabSyn's difficulties.

D1.justification: v2 discloses D1's prevalence cutoff of 1.6e-5, D2's code-type counts, MIR threshold 3, use of Yan et al.'s privacy-evaluation code, and settings/default implementations for TabDDPM and TabSyn. The cutoff and MIR threshold are newly documented, without evidence that existing experiments changed those settings. EHR-D3PM hardware and training details remain.

R1.justification: Related work now explicitly positions EHR-D3PM against general tabular diffusion, adding STaSy, CoDi and TabSyn references. Additional citations support medical tokenization, guidance and heterogeneous EHR modeling; Duan et al.'s membership-inference reference is removed. These are focused extensions of the existing positioning, rather than a redefinition of novelty.

P1.justification: v2 selectively rewrites related work, problem formulation, guidance explanations and experimental discussion, adds Broader Impacts and Limitations sections, and changes author order. The overall Sections 1–6 and Appendices A–C organization and much of the existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is extensively reorganized: D2 plots move into the main text, MIMIC/D1 plots move to appendices, and comparator panels are replaced. D2 count plots expand their range from 90 to 175. Tables are restyled and consolidated, fidelity and privacy are separated, and existing appendix uncertainties become visible in main-text tables.

improvement.justification: The added tabular-diffusion comparisons and attribute-inference tests strengthen the empirical assessment, while explicit temporal limitations and more qualified privacy interpretation improve its calibration. The gain is limited by qualitative-only dimensionality checks, unexplained new uncertainty terms, and average-improvement statements in Section 5.4 that remain inconsistent with the corresponding tables.
